newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Izetbegovic-Milosevic to boost Dayton in Paris.
newsitem.headline: Izetbegovic-Milosevic to boost Dayton in Paris.

text.p: Presidents Alija Izetbegovic of Bosnia and Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia meet on Thursday in Paris to boost the Dayton peace process and diplomats expect them to agree on a quick exchange of diplomatic missions.
"It is likely the two presidents will agree to open missions in Belgrade and Sarajevo shortly," a senior western diplomat posted in Belgrade told Reuters.
The two presidents had already agreed to "urgently" establish diplomatic relations when the countries recognized each other in Dayton, Ohio, last November.
Their meeting will be followed by lunch with French President Jacques Chirac and Carl Bildt, Swedish chief international civilian representative in Bosnia.
Izetbegovic and Milosevic are to discuss building peace after Bosnia's elections and normalising relations between the two countries, French officials said.

The results of elections in Bosnia on September 14, a cornerstone of the Dayton peace process, were certified on Sunday, clearing the way for formation of the new Bosnian multi-ethnic governing bodies.
It also paved way for the ending of U.N. sanctions against Yugoslavia, one of Belgrade's preconditions for the talks in Paris to take place.
Izetbegovic, who emerged top in the presidential elections, will serve as the Presidency's Chairman for the next two years and represent the country abroad.
When Milosevic and Izetbegovic face each other across the table in Paris it will be a meeting of old adversaries who now need each other.

Milosevic was instrumental in securing the Dayton peace accord by forcing the recalcitrant Bosnian Serb leaders to the negotiating table, thereby helping Izetbegovic preserve Bosnia, albeit as a loose union of two entities.
He will also be useful to Izetbegovic by reining in Serb members of the future joint Bosnian governnment who pay lip service to Dayton while making no secret of separatist desires.

Milosevic, on the other hand, needs good relations with Bosnia in keeping with the Dayton peace accord to restore Yugoslavia's position in international financial institutions. He also needs trade with Bosnia to boost his faltering economy.

Diplomats believe the dispute over Sarajevo's lawsuit before the Court of Justice in The Hague over alleged Serbian aggression against Bosnia might force the two presidents to stop short of agreeing to open embassies and instead opt for only bureaux for the time being.
Yugoslav Foreign Minister Milan Milutinovic told Sarajevo last Friday diplomatic relations cannot not be established with the lawsuit still in place, Bosnian Television reported.
But Bosnian officials said they would press the case.
"We have not got a single reason to drop the charge. That is an issue of law and Milosevic made a political issue of it," Mirza Hajric, Izetbegovic's adviser told Reuters.
Diplomats believe the two sides will eventually come to an agreement, given enough pressure."

Diplomats expect the two to set a date for the resumption of flights between Belgrade and Sarajevo, another step envisaged by the Dayton accord and recently agreed in Belgrade and Sarajevo by visiting trade delegations.
"The meeting is not expected to yield spectacular results," the diplomat said. "It is rather designed to be yet another sure step in shoring up the Dayton peace process."
